processing: Details of the old recipe are not recorded. As with other private Yiwu houses of the period, it was sun-dried leaf steamed and stone-pressed into round cakes, then aged by time alone.
harvest_season: Not documented for this house. Yiwu teas of the time drew on the surrounding mountains, and spring leaf is generally the most prized in pu-erh.
appearance_dry: Surviving old cakes are typically dark brown and compact with age, as is usual for pre-1950 pu-erh.
appearance_liquor: Deep chestnut to dark amber, which is what decades-old raw pu-erh typically gives.
appearance_wet: Dark brown, soft and fragile leaf, as is typical of very old raw pu-erh.
taste_profile: Few people have drunk it and there is no dependable tasting record. Very old raw pu-erh in general leans woody and earthy with a soft, smooth body.

brewing.notes: General advice for very old raw pu-erh, using boiling or nearly boiling water and a short rinse. Modern cakes with this name are ordinary young raw tea and should be treated as such.

vintage_note: Original cakes are antiques from the private tea-house era and change hands almost only through specialist auctions. Tea sold today under the name is modern production with no proven line back to the old house, so judge it by its own year and leaf.
description:
Fuyuanchang was one of the private family tea houses of Yiwu, in the old six famous mountains area of southern Yunnan. Its name is now shorthand for the top of the pu-erh collecting world, and it is usually listed with Songpin and Tongqing among the great haoji names.

Very little is on record about how it made its tea. Assume the general method of the time, leaf from the mountains around Yiwu pressed into round cakes, rather than any secret recipe.

The practical point for a drinker is that almost nobody will brew an original cake. Modern cakes that borrow old house names are often little more than white labels, so the name alone tells you nothing about what is inside.

If the name draws you, buy a good modern Yiwu cake from a producer who states the year and the origin of the leaf. That teaches you more about the region than a borrowed label will.
history:
The early dates are unsettled and rest mostly on later commercial accounts. A brand listing says the predecessor, Yuanchang Hao, was founded in the early Guangxu reign, in 1879, and that Yu Fusheng later took it over and renamed it Fuyuanchang. A Taiwanese magazine places Yuanchang in Yibang and Fuyuanchang on Yiwu's main street, saying Yu founded it in the Republican period and that it reopened in 1921.

The firm belongs to the period before state tea factories, when Han Chinese family businesses in Yiwu sold tea on to distant markets. Auction houses today class it among the haoji teas, those made by private houses from the Qing dynasty through the Republic.
